title: The Guarantee Stack: The Personal Exposure That Grows With Every Finance Facility You Sign
excerpt: Every equipment loan, overdraft and invoice facility usually comes with a personal guarantee attached. Most owners have never added up what all of them total together.
content:
Most SME owners can tell you the outstanding balance on every loan the business carries, often to the dollar. Far fewer can tell you, without checking, the total amount they have personally guaranteed to repay if the business cannot. Each facility gets signed on its own, usually at a moment focused on getting the finance approved rather than on what is actually being promised in the paperwork underneath it.

An equipment loan two years ago. An overdraft opened last year to smooth a slow quarter. An invoice finance facility added this year to fund a growth run. None of these decisions felt large in isolation. Taken together, they can add up to a personal exposure that is worth sitting down and actually totalling, rather than estimating from memory.

The pattern we see across owner-led businesses is that this total gets calculated once, properly, and it is almost always a lender, an investor or a family solicitor who asks for it first. Working it out before someone else does changes the conversation completely.

Why Guarantees Don't Retire When the Loan Does

Many guarantees are not limited to the single facility they were signed alongside, which surprises most owners when they hear it. An all monies guarantee, or a continuing guarantee, covers not just the loan on the table at the time but any future lending the business takes on with that institution, including facilities opened years later with a different manager and no fresh conversation about what is at stake. Paying off the original loan does not automatically release the guarantee behind it unless the lender confirms that release in writing.

This matters most at the exact moment a business is trying to grow. A new facility gets added to fund stock, a vehicle or a season of expansion, and the guarantee behind it stacks on top of whatever is already outstanding elsewhere, rather than quietly replacing it.

What the Stack Looks Like From the Other Side of the Table

A lender assessing a new application does not look only at the business's numbers. They look at the owner's total personal exposure across every guarantee currently on record, because that figure affects what is realistically recoverable if something goes wrong. A spouse who co-signed years ago as a formality can carry live exposure long after they stopped being involved in the business day to day, and most families only discover this when a facility comes up for renewal.

The same stack resurfaces at the exact moments a business most needs a clean position. Preparing for a capital raise brings every existing guarantee into the due diligence conversation, and an exposure nobody has mapped slows the process down right when momentum matters most to a lender or investor deciding whether to move forward.

The stack shows up again at the other end of the ownership cycle, when a business is sold. A buyer's solicitor will not let settlement proceed until every personal guarantee tied to the business's facilities has been formally released by the lender, and arranging that release can take several weeks once a bank is asked. Discovering this gap partway through a sale process, when timelines are already tight and a buyer is waiting on a settlement date, is one of the more avoidable ways a deal loses momentum in its final weeks.

Mapping It Before Someone Else Does

The fix is not complicated, it is just rarely done. List every facility the business currently holds, the guarantee attached to each one, whether it is capped at a specific amount or open ended, and whether it covers that single facility or all lending with that institution. Most owners who do this exercise for the first time find at least one guarantee they had assumed was closed out years ago, usually attached to a loan that was repaid long before anyone thought to ask the lender for a formal release.

This is also the right moment to test whether facilities set up years ago still earn their place, now that the business looks different to how it did when they were arranged, and to understand what the full capital stack actually looks like before approaching a new lender or investor with a fresh request. A structured banking and facility review gives an independent read on exactly this, scoped and priced before anything new gets signed, rather than discovered for the first time when a lender, an investor or a buyer's solicitor asks the question directly.

The businesses that handle this well treat the guarantee stack the way they treat any other liability on the balance sheet, something reviewed on a schedule rather than discovered under pressure. If it has been a while since anyone looked at the full picture across every facility the business carries, that is worth fixing before the next one gets added, not after. If it would help to talk it through, book a discovery call and bring the list of facilities with you.

faqs.q: What is a personal guarantee on a business loan in Australia?
faqs.a: A personal guarantee is a promise from a director or owner to repay a business debt personally if the business cannot. It sits alongside the loan itself and often extends to the owner's personal assets, including the family home, depending on how the guarantee is worded. Most bank and equipment finance facilities for SMEs require one.

faqs.q: Do personal guarantees end automatically when a business loan is repaid?
faqs.a: Not always. Continuing or all monies guarantees stay in place to cover future lending with that same institution, not just the facility they were signed alongside. Paying off the original loan does not release the guarantee unless the lender confirms the release in writing, which is why checking the actual wording matters more than assuming.

faqs.q: Can a spouse be held liable under a business loan personal guarantee?
faqs.a: Yes, if they signed as a co-guarantor, which happens often when a bank asks for both partners on a facility. That exposure can remain live for years, even after a spouse has stepped back from the business entirely. It is worth both parties knowing exactly what is signed, not assuming it is a formality.

faqs.q: How do I find out my total personal guarantee exposure across multiple lenders?
faqs.a: Start by listing every current facility, then request confirmation from each lender of the exact guarantee attached, including whether it is capped or open ended. Many owners find this clearer with an outside set of eyes across the full picture, which is the kind of work a banking and facility review is built to do.

faqs.q: Does a personal guarantee affect a business owner's ability to raise capital later?
faqs.a: It can. Investors and new lenders typically want full visibility of existing guarantees as part of due diligence, and an unclear or undocumented stack slows that process down. Mapping the position early, before approaching a new lender or investor, keeps the conversation moving rather than stalling on unanswered questions.

faqs.q: Is a director's guarantee the same thing as a personal guarantee?
faqs.a: Largely yes. A director's guarantee is simply a personal guarantee given in a director's capacity rather than as a private individual, though the practical effect on personal liability is the same either way. The label on the document matters less than the actual terms of what is being guaranteed.

faqs.q: Should I review my business's finance facilities before taking on new debt?
faqs.a: Yes, and before adding any new facility is the ideal time, not after. A review of existing terms, covenants and guarantees often reveals facilities that no longer suit the business or guarantees still attached to debt long since repaid, which is exactly the gap a fractional CFO engagement is designed to close.
